1.title: When Two Balls Meet
1.text:
When Two Balls Meet

In a collision, two objects exert equal and opposite forces, and equal and opposite impulses, on each other.

Our big question for this lesson: what is recoil and how is it useful? Let's start with two balls rolling toward each other, like the ones in Figure 9.

When they collide, each ball briefly pushes on the other. The balls have different sizes and speeds, but Newton's third law says the forces are equal and opposite: F red on blue equals negative F blue on red.

And here's a neat consequence. Both forces act for exactly the same time interval, so the impulses are also equal in size and opposite in direction: F red on blue times delta t equals negative F blue on red times delta t. Notice we never mentioned mass! Different sizes, different speeds, maybe different masses, and still the forces and impulses match.

testIt.name: Two balls meet
testIt.how: Tap to switch which ball is bigger. The forces on the two balls are always equal and opposite.

2.title: Momentum Before and After
2.text:
Momentum Before and After

In an isolated two-object collision, the momentum one object gains equals the momentum the other loses.

How do the balls' momenta change? Look at Figure 10. By the impulse-momentum theorem, for ball C, p sub C f minus p sub C i equals F D on C times delta t. For ball D, p sub D f minus p sub D i equals F C on D times delta t.

Because those impulses are equal and opposite, p sub C f minus p sub C i equals the negative of the quantity p sub D f minus p sub D i. Rearrange, and you get p sub C f plus p sub D f equals p sub C i plus p sub D i.

So the total momentum of the two balls is the same before and after the collision! The momentum ball D gains is exactly the momentum ball C loses. You can see the impulses match in Figure 10 because the force arrows during the collision are the same length.

testIt.name: Momentum bars
testIt.how: Set the masses and speeds. In a sticky collision the total momentum before equals after.

4.title: Closed, Isolated Systems
4.text:
Closed, Isolated Systems

The law of conservation of momentum states that the momentum of any closed, isolated system does not change.

When is a system's momentum conserved? First, no objects can leave or join the system. A system that doesn't gain or lose mass is a closed system. Second, the only forces must be internal forces, with no unbalanced forces from outside. When the net external force on a closed system is zero, it's an isolated system.

No system on Earth is perfectly isolated, since there's always some interaction with the surroundings. But often those interactions are small enough to ignore. Systems can have any number of objects, and objects can stick together or break apart, and momentum is still conserved. The law of conservation of momentum says the momentum of any closed, isolated system does not change.

That's powerful, because it connects before and after without knowing any details of the interaction. And if a system isn't isolated, its momentum can change, but that change is balanced by changes in the momentum of objects outside it.

testIt.how: Tap to change the system boundary and sort each force as internal or external.

5.title: Example Problem 3, Cars Stuck Together
5.text:
Example Problem 3, Cars Stuck Together

When objects stick together, v sub f equals the total initial momentum divided by the total mass.

A 1875-kilogram car going 23 meters per second rear-ends a 1025-kilogram compact car going 17 meters per second on ice in the same direction. The two cars stick together. How fast do they move right after the collision?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Define the system, set up a coordinate system, sketch the before and after states, and draw a momentum vector diagram. Known: m sub C equals 1875 kilograms, m sub D equals 1025 kilograms, v sub C i equals positive 23 meters per second, and v sub D i equals positive 17 meters per second. Unknown: v sub f.

Step two: solve. The system is the two cars. The ice makes the external force nearly zero, so momentum is conserved: p sub C i plus p sub D i equals p sub C f plus p sub D f, which means m sub C v sub C i plus m sub D v sub D i equals m sub C v sub C f plus m sub D v sub D f. The cars stick together, so they share one final velocity, v sub f. So m sub C v sub C i plus m sub D v sub D i equals the quantity m sub C plus m sub D, times v sub f. Solving, v sub f equals the total initial momentum divided by the total mass: 1875 kilograms times positive 23 meters per second plus 1025 kilograms times positive 17 meters per second, all divided by 1875 kilograms plus 1025 kilograms. That's positive 21 meters per second.

Step three: evaluate. Velocity is in meters per second. Both cars started moving in the positive direction, so v sub f should be positive. And 21 meters per second is between the two starting speeds, closer to the heavier car's speed. Makes sense!

testIt.name: Cars stuck together
testIt.how: Change the cars' speeds. They stick and share one velocity.

6.title: Recoil
6.text:
Recoil

Recoil is the backward motion of an object that pushes another object away; the two momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction.

Defining the system carefully matters. Look at the in-line skaters in Figure 11, on a smooth surface with no outside forces. Both start at rest, one behind the other. The boy, skater C, pushes the girl, skater D. Now they roll apart in opposite directions.

The push is an internal force, so momentum is conserved. The total momentum was zero before, so it's zero after: 0 equals p sub C f plus p sub D f, so p sub C f equals negative p sub D f, and m sub C v sub C f equals negative m sub D v sub D f. Choose right as positive. The boy's backward motion is called recoil.

Are their velocities equal and opposite? Solve for the boy's velocity: v sub C f equals negative m sub D over m sub C, times v sub D f. So it depends on their masses. If the boy is 68.0 kilograms and the girl is 45.4 kilograms, the girl moves 1.50 times as fast as the boy. The lighter skater always moves faster. That's how you can tell in Figure 11 that the boy is heavier: the girl moved farther forward than he moved back, compared to the red ball in the background. That ball is a fixed reference point that lets you measure motion. But without knowing how hard he pushed, you can't find either speed.

testIt.name: Push apart
testIt.how: Set the skaters' masses and tap to push apart. Total momentum stays zero.

7.title: Propulsion in Space
7.text:
Propulsion in Space

A rocket accelerates in space by pushing exhaust out one way so that it recoils the other way.

How does a rocket change velocity in space, with nothing to push against? It carries fuel and oxidizer. When they combine in the motor, hot gases shoot out the nozzle at high speed. The rocket and its chemicals form a closed system, and the forces pushing out the gas are internal, so the system is isolated too. By conservation of momentum and Newton's third law, the gas goes one way and the rocket goes the other. That's recoil at work!

A newer kind of space propulsion uses the recoil from ions. An ion thruster accelerates ions in an electric or magnetic field. As the ions are thrown out one way, the spacecraft moves the opposite way. Animators in movies and video games use these same laws of motion to make spaceship crashes look believable.

testIt.name: Rocket motor
testIt.how: Set the gas mass and its speed and tap to fire. The rocket gains the momentum the gas carries away.

8.title: Example Problem 4, The Thruster Pistol
8.text:
Example Problem 4, The Thruster Pistol

For a system that starts at rest, m sub C v sub C f equals negative m sub D v sub D f.

An astronaut at rest in space fires a thruster pistol that shoots out a quick burst of 35 grams of hot gas at 875 meters per second. The astronaut and pistol together have a mass of 84 kilograms. How fast, and which way, is the astronaut moving afterward?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Define the system and a coordinate axis, sketch before and after, and draw a vector diagram. Known: m sub C equals 84 kilograms, m sub D equals 0.035 kilograms, v sub C i and v sub D i both equal 0.0 meters per second, and v sub D f equals negative 875 meters per second. Unknown: v sub C f.

Step two: solve. The system is the astronaut, the pistol, and the gas. Before firing, everything is at rest, so the initial momentum is 0.0 kilogram meters per second. Conservation of momentum says 0.0 equals p sub C f plus p sub D f, so p sub C f equals negative p sub D f. The astronaut's momentum matches the gas's in size, but points the other way. Then m sub C v sub C f equals negative m sub D v sub D f, so v sub C f equals negative m sub D v sub D f over m sub C: negative 0.035 kilograms times negative 875 meters per second, divided by 84 kilograms, which is positive 0.36 meters per second.

Step three: evaluate. The velocity is in meters per second. The astronaut moves opposite the gas. And the astronaut is far more massive than the gas, so the astronaut moves much more slowly. That's how recoil is useful: it can steer an astronaut, or a whole spacecraft.

testIt.name: Thruster pistol
testIt.how: Tap to fire. The 84 kg astronaut drifts the other way.

9.title: Collisions in Two Dimensions
9.text:
Collisions in Two Dimensions

In a two-dimensional collision, momentum is conserved separately in the x direction and in the y direction.

Conservation of momentum works no matter which directions things move. Look at the billiard balls in Figure 12. Ball C rolls in with momentum p sub C i, and ball D sits still. So the system's momentum before the collision is just p sub C i. Ignoring friction with the table, the system is closed and isolated.

After the collision, both balls move, and p sub C i equals p sub C f plus p sub D f, as vectors. Let the x-axis point along the initial momentum. Then the initial y-component is zero, so the final y-components must add to zero: p sub C f, y plus p sub D f, y equals 0. They're equal in size and opposite in sign. And the x-components still add up: p sub C i equals p sub C f, x plus p sub D f, x.

What if the balls roll on a thick carpet? Then friction from the carpet is an outside force, so the two balls' momentum isn't conserved. The momentum they lose goes into the carpet and the floor, and through them to Earth, so the change is balanced outside the system.

testIt.name: Pool shot
testIt.how: Set the angle the cue ball deflects. Equal-mass balls: the vector sum of the momenta is unchanged.

10.title: Example Problem 5, A Collision at an Intersection
10.text:
Example Problem 5, A Collision at an Intersection

The final momentum's size is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components, and its angle is the inverse tangent of p sub y over p sub x.

A 1325-kilogram car, C, heading north at 27.0 meters per second, collides with a 2165-kilogram car, D, heading east at 11.0 meters per second. They stick together. In what direction, and how fast, do they move?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Define the system, sketch before and after, put the y-axis north and the x-axis east, and draw a momentum vector diagram. Known: m sub C equals 1325 kilograms, m sub D equals 2165 kilograms, v sub C i, y equals 27.0 meters per second, and v sub D i, x equals 11.0 meters per second. Unknown: v sub f and the angle theta.

Step two: solve. The system is the two cars. Car C's momentum is 1325 kilograms times 27.0 meters per second, or 3.58 times 10 to the fourth kilogram meters per second north. Car D's momentum is 2165 kilograms times 11.0 meters per second, or 2.38 times 10 to the fourth kilogram meters per second east. Momentum is conserved in each direction, so p sub f, x equals 2.38 times 10 to the fourth, and p sub f, y equals 3.58 times 10 to the fourth. The total, p sub f, is the square root of the square of p sub f, x plus the square of p sub f, y, which is 4.30 times 10 to the fourth kilogram meters per second. The angle is theta equals the inverse tangent of 3.58 times 10 to the fourth over 2.38 times 10 to the fourth, or 56.4 degrees north of east. Finally, the speed is v sub f equals p sub f over the quantity m sub C plus m sub D: 4.30 times 10 to the fourth kilogram meters per second over 3490 kilograms, which is 12.3 meters per second.

Step three: evaluate. Speed is in meters per second. The answers are positive and the angle points between north and east, as it should. And since the cars stick together, v sub f must be smaller than car C's starting speed. It is!

testIt.name: Intersection
testIt.how: Set both speeds. The momentum triangle gives the wreck's speed and direction.

11.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum
11.text:
Conservation of Angular Momentum

If no net external torque acts on a closed system, its angular momentum does not change: L sub i equals L sub f.

Angular momentum can be conserved too. The law of conservation of angular momentum says that if no net external torque acts on a closed system, its angular momentum doesn't change: L sub i equals L sub f.

Watch the skater in Figure 13. When he pulls in his arms, he spins faster. With no outside torque, his angular momentum, L equals I omega, stays constant. Pulling in his arms brings mass closer to the axis, which lowers his moment of inertia, so his angular velocity has to go up.

You can calculate it: I sub i omega sub i equals I sub f omega sub f, so omega sub f over omega sub i equals I sub i over I sub f. Halve the moment of inertia, and the spin rate doubles!

testIt.how: Tap to pull the skater's arms in or out and watch ω.

12.title: Tops and Precession
12.text:
Tops and Precession

Precession is the slow circling of a spinning object's rotation axis, caused by a torque.

Because angular momentum is conserved, only a torque can change the direction a spinning object's axis points. Think of a top. When it stands straight up, gravity on its center of mass points right through the pivot, so there's no torque, and its axis stays put.

But tip the top, as in Figure 14, and gravity makes a torque that tries to rotate it downward. Instead of falling over, the top's axis slowly precesses: its upper end sweeps around in a circle about the vertical line. That's why a top precesses only when it's tilted. No tilt, no torque!

Earth precesses too. It isn't a perfect sphere. It bulges at the equator, so the gravitational pulls of the Sun and the Moon make a torque on it. It takes about 26,000 years for Earth's axis to go once around its precession circle.

testIt.name: Precessing top
testIt.how: Set the tilt and tap to spin the top. Gravity's torque turns the axis around instead of tipping it over.

13.title: Gyroscopes and Spirals
13.text:
Gyroscopes and Spirals

A gyroscope is a rapidly spinning wheel or disk whose axis keeps its direction unless a torque acts on it.

A gyroscope, like the one in Figure 15, is a wheel or disk that spins fast around one axis while it's free to turn around one or two other axes. Its large angular momentum can only change direction if the right torque acts on it. So airplanes, submarines, and spacecraft use gyroscopes to keep a fixed reference direction. Unlike a magnetic compass, a gyroscopic compass keeps working even when it isn't level.

Quarterbacks use the gyroscope effect too. In a spiral pass, the football spins around its long axis. Thrown along that spin axis, it keeps its pointy end forward, cutting air resistance so it flies far and true. If the spin is a bit off, it wobbles. If there's no spin, it tumbles end over end. Spin also steadies a flying disk, and a fast-spinning yo-yo stays in one plane, which makes tricks possible.

So what's recoil, and why is it useful? Recoil is the backward motion an object gets when it pushes something else away, because the total momentum has to stay the same. It's what lets rockets, ion thrusters, and astronauts with thruster pistols move through space.

testIt.how: Set the spin and tap the frame to tilt it. A fast gyroscope keeps pointing the same way.
